title: Intersectional Sycophancy: How Perceived User Demographics Shape False Validation in Large Language Models

live_model.evidence: Sec. 3.1: "Target models: (1) GPT-5-nano (OpenAI) and (2) Claude Haiku 4.5"; Abstract: "GPT-5-nano scores far higher...avg sycophancy 2.96 vs 1.74"

prompt.location: Sec. 3.1 (auditor/target/judge behavior described); Appendix F (one example transcript); exact templates live inside Anthropic's "Petri" tool, not reprinted here
prompt.note: Three-model pipeline: auditor=GPT-5-mini (persona with false belief), target=GPT-5-nano (evaluated for sycophancy), judge=GPT-5.1 (37-dim rubric, Petri).

claim.metric: average sycophancy score (1-10 scale, judge rubric), GPT-5-nano
claim.location: Abstract ("average sycophancy scores of x̄=2.96 vs. 1.74"); n_items = 768 total conversations / 2 target models = 384 for GPT-5-nano (128 personas x 3 domains, up to 40 turns each, mean 21.5)

data.source: Anthropic's Petri framework (public red-teaming/auditing tool, Fronsdal et al. 2025); 128 persona combinations x 3 domains defined in the paper

notes: Marked 'maybe': GPT-5-nano (target, role S) and GPT-5-mini (auditor) are both on the live list, but the exact conversational templates and the 37-dimension judge rubric are implemented inside the external Petri tool rather than fully reprinted in the paper, and the judge model (GPT-5.1) is not one of the tracked still-callable snapshots (though nothing indicates it is retired/dead). Topic is AI-safety sycophancy research (false beliefs about math/philosophy/conspiracy theories), not a request for genuinely harmful content, so the tos rule was not applied. est_calls is a rough estimate (384 conversations x ~21.5 turns x target+auditor calls, plus 384 judge calls).
